question: The findings of a Eurostat report on unmet needs for medical examinations look bleak for Greece. The country ranks first in terms of self-reported unmet needs for medical examinations due to financial reasons, long waiting lists or distance from healthcare facilities. In 2022, 3.3% of people in need of medical examinations across the EU were not able to undergo them because they could not afford to.

The EU countries reporting the highest values were: Greece (16.7%), Finland (9.6%), Romania (7.9%) and Latvia (7.1%). The share of people at risk of poverty in the EU who reported such unmet needs was 6.1%, which is twice as high as those not at risk (2.8%). In Greece, the reported share was 14.5 percentage points higher among those at risk of poverty (28.8%) compared with those not at risk (14.3%).

Wide discrepancies were also seen in Romania (15.5% compared with 6.1%) and in Portugal (11.7% compared with 3.2%). What initiatives will the Commission take in order to ensure that all EU citizens, particularly those at risk of poverty, have access to essential medical examinations?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.3.2024) The Commission has mentioned the concerns about unmet medical needs in the EU Health Synthesis Report 2023 123 and the European Semester Country Report Greece 20234. Reducing poverty is part of the European Pillar of Social Rights.

Greece aims at reducing the number of persons at risk of poverty or social exclusion (AROPE) by 860 000 and the share of children AROPE by 6.6 percentage points. Two actions under the EU4Health programme will provide policy guidance on how to mitigate the risk of poverty through reducing the impact of out-of-pocket spending on healthcare5 and addressing health benefits across income groups6.

Through the Resilience and Recovery facility (RRF), more than EUR 41 billion are allocated for investment in health. Furthermore, over EUR 10 billion is planned to be spent on enhancing accessibility, effectiveness and resilience of health systems through the Cohesion Policy Funds7. In the case of Greece, through the RRF, over EUR 1.
486 billion are to be invested in health with a substantial part planned to support primary health care and National Healthcare System through infrastructure upgrade and digital transformation.

Through the Cohesion Policy funds, Greece has foreseen to invest around EUR 416 million from the European Regional Development Fund in health infrastructure, health equipment and e-health services and EUR 323 million from the European Social Fund Plus to improve the accessibility of health services, with a focus on marginalised communities, vulnerable groups and children.

The Greek action plan for the European Child Guarantee8 includes extending the Newborns Screening Programme, creating mobile units in remote areas and vouchers for transportation for special treatments.
